stem: Lip bumper with acrylic shield vs wire?
recalled_answer: 1. The lip bumper with an acrylic shield produced significantly higher resting forces than the wire lip bumper. 2. The position of the lip bumper significantly affected the force at the molars: higher at 4 mm anterior vs 2 mm, and at 4 mm gingival vs the middle of the clinical crown. 3. No significant differences because of gender, malocclusion, facial pattern, or lip thickness.

verified.answer: The shield (acrylic) lip bumper gave significantly higher resting forces than the wire lip bumper (p<0.001; 43% higher at 4M, 25% higher at 4G). Force also rose when the bumper sat 4 mm rather than 2 mm in front of the incisors, and 4 mm gingival rather than at mid-crown. Sex, malocclusion, FMA pattern and lip thickness made no significant difference.
verified.where: Hodge et al 1997, Conclusions 1-3 (p621); Results 'Comparison of forces with and without the shield' (p616); Discussion 'Effect of a shield' (p620); Fig 6
verified.explanation: The recalled answer matches the paper's three conclusions almost exactly. Two caveats: overbite groups did differ significantly (Table III, p<0.01), and left vs right sides also differed (p<0.01). The shield was tested only at 4 mm, because its own thickness already put it 4 mm forward.

Maxillary spacing is linked separately to /l/, /n/, /d/. The paper names no single cause. The handwritten T-N-D matches these alveolar consonants.

verified.explanation: The paper names the greatest bone height around the cervical neck as the main factor in preventing black triangles. stem: Kokich canine article (Fig 5, photos A-C of an impacted maxillary canine): what is the appropriate exposure technique?
source_tag: Literature review articles (Kokich canine article Fig 5 pasted)

verified.answer: Early open exposure of a palatal canine: raise a full-thickness palatal flap, remove all bone down to the CEJ, then replace the flap with a window (hole) over the crown so the canine erupts on its own. No apically positioned flap.
verified.where: Kokich 2004 Fig 5 legend p 282 (A palatal impaction, B flap raised and crown under bone, C bone removed to the CEJ, D flap replaced with a hole); text p 283 (Kokich & Mathews early uncovering; eruption to the occlusal plane in 6-8 months)
verified.explanation: Fig 5 is the palatal case, and the technique shown is early uncovering with full bone removal and a fenestrated replaced flap, followed by free eruption. The paper describes the apically positioned flap only for labial canines (Figs 2-3). The recalled 'apical positioning flap' fits only if the pasted figure was really Fig 2 or 3.

stem: Kokich missing premolar article (Fig 1: submerged-looking retained deciduous mandibular second molar, radiograph, occlusal view): management?

verified.answer: Reduce the E's mesiodistal width, protect it with composite and maintain it, closing the residual space to keep the ridge for a later implant
verified.where: Kokich & Kokich 2006 Patient 1 p 437 (12 y 4 mo girl; E 13 mm wide vs 7.5 mm for a premolar; flat bone levels mean not ankylosed); Fig 1 legend p 438; reduction technique pp 441-442 (about 2 mm off each side)
verified.explanation: In Fig 1 the deciduous molar was not ankylosed (flat interproximal bone), so it was narrowed, built up with composite and kept to preserve buccolingual bone until growth ended. This is exactly the recalled answer.

stem: Case of Class I malocclusion with 4 mm lower crowding, Bolton (anterior) excess, less keratinized gingiva at the lower left canine and normal profile. Extraction pattern?

stem: For lower central incisor extraction, which tooth to choose?

stem: 25-year-old who did not have orthodontic treatment before came complaining of retrusion of the lips after 10 years. Why?

stem: Patient concerned about mini-screw: which site is the best in the maxilla?

verified.answer: b) Between 6 and 5 at 8 mm

verified.explanation: The 6-5 interradicular space is the top maxillary safe site up to 8 mm from the crest; palatally it measures 4.6 mm at 8 mm. The 4-3 space is listed as safe only from 5 to 11 mm; at 2 mm it is just 3.0 mm, under the 3.1 mm threshold. So 'all levels' is wrong.

stem: Which jaw has a higher (mini-screw) failure rate?

verified.answer: Mandible
verified.where: Park 2006 Table III (p22): maxilla 96.0% vs mandible 86.4% success, p=.01; Tables IV-V odds ratios; Discussion and Conclusions (p23-25)
verified.explanation: Screws in the mandible failed more often than in the maxilla, against the authors' expectation. They suggest overheating of dense bone during drilling and food irritation of posterior screws. Chen 2009 also reports higher survival in the maxilla.

stem: Class II div 1 with increased overjet and mild crowding in the lower arch, lower second molars not yet erupted. What is the best extraction pattern?

verified.answer: c) U4's and L5's
verified.where: George 2021, Methods inclusion criteria (p334); Discussion p337 and p340; Abstract conclusion (p333)
verified.explanation: The stem matches George's sample: growing Class II div 1, mild or no crowding, permanent dentition without second molars. George concludes that 4/5 extraction helps Class II molar correction (more lower molar protraction) and keeps the lower incisors in place, whereas 4/4 over-retracts them and can make overjet and profile worse. One caveat: Janson 2009 (same topic) suggests upper-4s-only may be preferred when lower crowding is little to moderate, but the second-molar cue points to George.

stem: 15-year-old with Class II div 1 with increased overjet and mild crowding in the lower arch, lower second molar not erupted yet. What is the best extraction pattern?

verified.explanation: For a growing Class II div 1 with mild crowding and acceptable lower incisor position, George shows that 4/5 extraction protracts the lower molars more (+0.7 mm) and retracts the lower incisors less, which helps the Class II molar correction without flattening the profile. Neither pattern changed the mandibular plane angle (no 'wedge effect'). Janson 2009 would argue for upper 4s only when lower crowding is minimal, but the wording follows George's sample.

stem: Patient came for extraction of a lower incisor. Which incisor / how?

verified.explanation: An elastic chain tips the chosen incisor lingually to about 45° while the space in front of it closes. Options b and c are the opposite of the paper's advice: choose the most bone, and avoid the labially displaced tooth.

verified.answer: d) Equal pattern

verified.where: Burkhardt 2003, Abstract p108; Results p112 and Table IV p112 (MPA +1.2° pendulum vs slight closure in both Herbst groups, P<.01; Co-Gn 6.2 vs 6.4 vs 6.4 mm, NS); Conclusions p115
verified.explanation: Over the full treatment the pendulum group's mandibular plane angle opened by about 1.2°, while both Herbst groups closed slightly. The difference was significant. Mandibular length gains did not differ significantly among the three groups, so options a, b and c (less or more growth or length than Herbst) are not supported.

stem: Which is correct regarding U4s vs U&L4s extraction?
options: a. U4s is more stable long term
b. U&L4s is more stable long term
c. U4s has more increase in apical base
d. U&L4s has more increase in apical base
recalled_answer: c. U4s has more increase in apical base
source_tag: 10, 5 Long-term stability of Class II malocclusion treated with 2- and 4-premolar extraction protocols, Guilherme Janson

verified.answer: c. U4s has more increase in apical base
verified.where: Janson 2009, Abstract (p154.e1); Table IV (p154.e6): ANB +1.08 vs +0.06°, P = 0.025; Conclusions (p154.e9)
verified.explanation: Janson found similar long-term stability for the 2- and 4-premolar protocols, so options a and b are wrong. The 2-maxillary-premolar group had more post-treatment forward maxillary displacement and a greater increase in the apical-base relationship (ANB), which the authors call too small to matter clinically.

stem: What is true regarding Forsus?
source_tag: 11, 5 Treatment and posttreatment effects induced by the Forsus appliance: A controlled clinical study, Giorgio Cacciatore

verified.answer: c. Minimal effect on maxilla (the paper supports this as the long-term answer; b is true only for the active-treatment period)
verified.where: Cacciatore 2014, Abstract (p1010); Table 2 (p1013), Table 4 (p1015); Conclusions (p1016)
verified.explanation: Over the full observation the Forsus corrected Class II mainly dentoalveolarly: overjet -3.8 mm and molar relationship +3.7 mm, with no significant skeletal change (net SNA -0.3°, NS). The maxillary restraint seen at the end of treatment (SNA -1.7°) was described as a slight headgear effect and largely relapsed. Option a is clearly wrong, but the question is ambiguous between b and c because the abstract does call the treatment-period maxillary restriction significant.

stem: 12-year-old boy with Class II malocclusion; you decided to treat him with a functional appliance. Which of the following is correct?
options: a. Short-term amount of supplementary mandibular growth
b. Long-term amount of supplementary mandibular growth
recalled_answer: a. Short term amount of supplementary mandibular growth
source_tag: 11, 1 Mandibular changes produced by functional appliances in Class II malocclusion: A systematic review, Paola Cozza

verified.answer: a. Short-term amount of supplementary mandibular growth (is significantly larger when treatment includes the pubertal growth spurt)
verified.where: Cozza 2006, Abstract p599.e1; Discussion p599.e9–e10 (all 'peak' samples ≥2 mm except Tümer, no prepeak sample clinically significant); Conclusion 3 p599.e11; only 1 of 22 studies (Faltin) followed patients to the end of growth, p599.e11
verified.explanation: The review says functional appliances produce supplementary mandibular growth in the short term, and that it is larger when treatment covers the pubertal peak (a 12-year-old boy is close to that window). It cannot speak to long-term supplementary growth, because only one included study followed patients to the end of growth.

stem: Patient was treated using Twin-block appliance, wearing it full time for one year. The orthopedic increase will be:
source_tag: 11, 1 Mandibular changes produced by functional appliances in Class II malocclusion: A systematic review, Paola Cozza (Twin-block coefficient of efficiency 0.23 mm/month; handwritten 0.23 x 12 = 2.76); 11, 4 Long-Term Dentoskeletal Changes with the Bionator, Herbst, Twin Block, and MARA Functional Appliances, Nicole J. Siara-Olds

verified.answer: c. 2.8 (derived: 0.23 mm/month × 12 months = 2.76 mm)
verified.where: Cozza 2006, Results p599.e6 and Discussion p599.e11 (Twin-block coefficient of efficiency 0.23 mm/month from 7 samples; Herbst 0.28, bionator 0.17, activator 0.12, Fränkel 0.09, average 0.16 mm/month); Table V p599.e10
verified.explanation: Cozza defines the coefficient of efficiency as the extra mandibular length over controls divided by months of active treatment. For the Twin-block this was 0.23 mm per month, so one year of full-time wear predicts about 2.76 mm, which rounds to 2.8 mm. The 12-month multiplication is derived; the paper itself reports only the per-month figure. Siara-Olds' Twin Block figure (~1.5 mm/year over controls) does not match any of the options.

stem: Question asking about the effect of the MARA appliance:
options: b. Results in steep mandibular plane
recalled_answer: b. Results in steep mandibular plane
source_tag: 11, 4 Long-Term Dentoskeletal Changes with the Bionator, Herbst, Twin Block, and MARA Functional Appliances, Nicole J. Siara-Olds

verified.answer: b. Results in steep mandibular plane (best option; the paper actually says Herbst and MARA gave a steeper occlusal plane, and MARA opened SN-GoGn vs controls during phase I)
verified.where: Siara-Olds 2010, Conclusions p28 (Herbst and MARA restricted maxillary growth and steepened the occlusal plane); Table 3 p22 (MARA SN-GoGn +0.93°/yr vs controls T2–T1, P=.01; IMPA +2.46°/yr, P=.0002); Discussion p28 (vertical increase explains MARA's SNB decrease; incisor flaring temporary)
verified.explanation: For MARA the paper reports temporary maxillary restriction, a steeper occlusal plane, and a phase-I increase in vertical dimension (SN-GoGn) that it blames for the drop in SNB, which fits option b. Options c (greatest vertical control) and d (greatest long-term lower-incisor flaring) describe the Twin Block. MARA's lower-incisor proclination was significant in phase I but had resolved by the end of fixed appliances. Option a contradicts the reported maxillary restriction. One caution: the conclusions say occlusal plane, not mandibular plane.

stem: 10-year-old boy presented with Class III malocclusion, prognathic mandible, deep bite, reverse overbite. (They had a table with Co-Gn and Co-Goi decreased, and Co-Pg and Ar-Goi-Me increased.)
options: a. Successful outcome with facemask treatment if done early
b. Ideal treatment will be provided if deferred to 11-13
d. Indicates better success would be provided with camouflage treatment
recalled_answer: a, b and c crossed out (X), leaving d. Indicates better success would be provided with camouflage treatment
source_tag: 12, 1 Cephalometric variables to predict future success of early orthopedic Class III treatment, Matthew A. Ghiz

verified.answer: The profile predicts an UNSUCCESSFUL early facemask outcome (relapse after pubertal growth). None of the recalled options states this. The paper links predicted failure to waiting for growth to finish (surgery), not to camouflage, so d is only the elimination choice (not stated in the paper)
verified.where: Ghiz 2005 Abstract (p301). Table II (p304). Discussion p304: the model helps choose between camouflage during growth and waiting for surgery. Limitations p305
verified.explanation: A decreased Co-GD (probably what 'Co-Gn' means here) and Co-Goi with an increased Co-Pg and gonial angle is the failure pattern, so a is wrong. Neither the 11-13 deferral (b) nor a 56% success rate (c) appears in the paper; its figures are 95.5% and 70% prediction accuracy. In the paper's logic, camouflage during growth goes with patients predicted to succeed, so d does not follow from it, though it may be the intended key.

stem: Two siblings presented to the clinic and will undergo expansion using Haas. What is the expected treatment outcome?
options: a. More nasal and lateronasal expansion is expected in older sibling
b. More intermolar expansion is expected in older sibling
c. More intermolar expansion is expected in younger sibling
source_tag: 15, 3 Long-Term Dental Arch Changes After Rapid Maxillary Expansion Treatment: A Systematic Review; 15, 4 Rapid Maxillary Expansion - Tooth Tissue-Borne Versus Tooth-Borne Expanders: A Computed Tomography Evaluation of Dentoskeletal Effects, Daniela G. Garib; handwritten '?' after stem

verified.answer: b. More intermolar expansion is expected in the older sibling
verified.where: t14_2 Results p158 (early 12.7 vs late 13.5 mm Um-Um) and Discussion/Conclusions p159 (0.8 mm difference; skeletal before peak, dentoalveolar after)
verified.explanation: Baccetti's Haas data, as reported in the review, show slightly more transverse dental change after puberty than before. The difference is about 0.8 mm and may not matter clinically. Skeletal expansion was larger in the younger, prepubertal group, which makes option a wrong.

stem: You decided to expand using a banded expander. Which tooth will have the most tipping?
source_tag: 15, 4 Rapid Maxillary Expansion - Tooth Tissue-Borne Versus Tooth-Borne Expanders: A Computed Tomography Evaluation of Dentoskeletal Effects, Daniela G. Garib

verified.answer: c. 2nd premolar
verified.where: t14_3 Table 5 p554 (P2 6.7°, P1 2.3°, M1 2.5°); Discussion p556; Conclusions p557
verified.explanation: The second premolars are not banded and are pushed only by the connecting bar, far from their centre of resistance. They therefore tipped buccally about 6.7°, roughly three times as much as the banded first premolars and first molars. This held in both the Haas and Hyrax groups.

stem: Which suture will open during expansion?
source_tag: 15, 2 Effects of rapid maxillary expansion on the cranial and circummaxillary sutures, Ahmed Ghoneima

verified.answer: d. Nasofrontal (frontonasal)
verified.where: t14_1 Abstract; Results p516-517; Table I p518 (frontonasal +0.2 mm, P<0.001)
verified.explanation: Ghoneima's CT data show significant widening of the frontonasal, internasal, nasomaxillary, frontomaxillary and intermaxillary sutures. The pterygomaxillary, zygomaticomaxillary, zygomaticotemporal and frontozygomatic sutures did not change significantly, which the authors put down to heavy interdigitation.

stem: Expected outcomes of treating a young girl with Haas?
options: d. Buccal displacement of the palatal shelves
recalled_answer: d. Buccal displacement of the palatal shelves
source_tag: 15, 4 Rapid Maxillary Expansion - Tooth Tissue-Borne Versus Tooth-Borne Expanders: A Computed Tomography Evaluation of Dentoskeletal Effects, Daniela G. Garib

verified.answer: d. Buccal displacement of the palatal shelves (lateral rotation of the maxillary halves)
verified.where: t14_3 Discussion p555 (lateral rotation of maxillary halves, fulcrum near frontomaxillary suture); Table 2 p553 (Haas group)
verified.explanation: Garib describes the hemimaxillae rotating outward, so the hard palate widened along with the teeth. The 5.5 mm figure in Table 2 is the buccal alveolar crest width at the molar, not molar (dental) expansion, which was about 7-8 mm. Garib also refutes the claim that one appliance is less stable. Option a is a plausible trap if the examiner read 5.5 mm as molar expansion.

stem: 18-year-old patient will be treated with a miniscrew-assisted palatal expander followed by clear aligners. Which of the following is the consequence?
options: b. More root resorption of the anchored teeth
c. Decrease in buccal bone thickness of anchored teeth
recalled_answer: All four options (a-d) crossed out (X); no answer marked
source_tag: 16, 3 Treatment of maxillary transversal deficiency by using a mini-implant-borne rapid maxillary expander and aligners in combination, Benedict Wilmes (excerpt: nearly 1:1 molar movement with screw turns; little relapse potential, no need for significant overcorrection; skeletal retainer can retain width)

verified.answer: d. Long retention period, in the sense that the expander can stay as a skeletal retainer for a relatively long time while aligners proceed (not stated as a 'consequence'; options a–c are contradicted by the paper)
verified.where: Wilmes 2021, Introduction (p 147): MARPE gives less root resorption, less buccal bone loss and no more pain. Discussion (p 151): aligners can start right after expansion with the expander kept for retention. p 152: a skeletal retainer can hold the width over a relatively long period.
verified.explanation: Wilmes says MARPE causes no more pain, less root resorption and less buccal-bone thinning of anchor teeth, so a, b and c are wrong. Its advantage with aligners is that the expander stays as a long-term skeletal retainer, so no separate retention phase delays treatment. Option d is therefore the only defensible answer. The resident marked no answer.

stem: 22-year-old patient with mild osteoporosis presented to the ortho-surgery clinic for correction of anterior open bite. Which is correct regarding relapse of the open bite?
source_tag: 17, 4 Stability of treatment for anterior open-bite malocclusion: A meta-analysis, Greenlee (handwritten note beside d: 'success rate')

verified.answer: d. More than 75%, read as success or stability: 82% of surgically treated patients kept a positive overbite at 1 year or more (75% for nonsurgical). That means only about 18% relapsed (derived).
verified.where: Abstract; Results p158 (secondary dichotomous analysis); Table VI; Conclusions p165
verified.explanation: Greenlee's pooled case series: surgical patients (mean age 23.3 years) went from -2.8 mm to +1.6 mm overbite and settled at +1.3 mm after 3.5 years. Option d works as the success rate, which matches the handwritten note. Read literally as a relapse rate, the paper would support 'less than 50%'. Osteoporosis is not discussed.

stem: Patient was treated with clear aligners for correction of deep bite. The main mechanism of correction was:
source_tag: 17, 2 Management of overbite with the Invisalign appliance, Roozbeh Khosravi

verified.answer: b. Proclination of L incisors
verified.where: Results p694; Fig 3 p695; Appendix Table II (L1-NB +1.6° median, P=0.02); Conclusions p699
verified.explanation: Khosravi names lower incisor proclination as the main way Invisalign opened the bite (median 1.5 mm). Upper incisor intrusion and slight lower molar extrusion were secondary. Levelling the curve of Spee was a clinician strategy, not a measured mechanism.

source_tag: 18, 2 Dynamic Smile Analysis: Changes with Age, Shyam G. Desai

stem: Patient presented with rotated lower incisors and moderate crowding. Which of the following is important for the stability of correction?
options: a. Place lateral incisors inside canines
source_tag: 19, 1 Important Aspects of Long-Term Stability, Bjorn U. Zachrisson (Early correction of rotations)

verified.answer: b. Early correction
verified.where: Zachrisson 1997, 'Early Correction of Rotations' (PDF p.3)
verified.explanation: Correcting rotations early, before transseptal fibres are established, should reduce rotational relapse. Lateral incisors 'inside' the canines contradicts Zachrisson (labial is advised), and fiberotomy is less successful in the lower arch.

stem: Patient was treated for a deep bite. What do you expect the relapse to be?
source_tag: 17, 3 The effectiveness and long-term stability of overbite correction with incisor intrusion mechanics, Huda Al-Buraiki

verified.answer: b. Insignificant. Overbite rose only 0.7 mm (17%) after treatment, which is statistically significant but clinically insignificant. Net correction was 3.3 mm and final overbite 2.6 mm.
verified.where: Abstract; Table VII p52; Discussion 'Stability of overbite correction' p54
verified.explanation: Al-Buraiki corrected a mean 5.9 mm deep bite by 4 mm with incisor intrusion mechanics. Years after retention, overbite came back by only 0.7 mm. That is lower than the 23-60% relapse in earlier studies, which the authors credit to long retention and a bite-plane retainer.

stem: Two brothers came after 10 years; one was treated with extraction of U&L4s while the other was treated non-extraction. Which of the following would be different?
recalled_answer: a. Lower incisor crowding crossed out (X); b. Overjet and c. Overbite carry unclear handwritten marks
source_tag: 7, 1 Long-term profile changes in extraction and nonextraction patients, Corbett K. Stephens

verified.answer: None of the listed features is shown to differ (not stated in the paper); lower incisor crowding in particular recurs after both protocols
verified.where: Stephens 2005 Table III p 453 and conclusion 1 p 457 (no long-term Ex vs Nonex differences in profile, U1-SN or L1-NB at about 15 years); Melrose t19_3 (topic 19): lower incisor crowding after retention follows extraction, serial extraction and nonextraction treatment
verified.explanation: Stephens finds the two groups alike 15 years later in profile and incisor inclination but never measures crowding, overjet or overbite, and Kouvelis covers skeletal vertical dimension, not overbite. The resident's crossing-out of (a) fits topic 19, but no paper settles (b) versus (c), and the recalled marks are unreadable.

source_tag: Proffit ch 20 (excerpt: if TMJ surgery is required along with jaw surgery, usually better to defer it until after the orthognathic surgery)
proffit_chapter: Ch 20 Combined surgical and orthodontic treatment

verified.answer: b. Perform TMJ surgery and orthognathic surgery simultaneously (Wolford). Proffit's key is c, defer TMJ surgery.
verified.where: Wolford 2001 p95-96 (TMJs must be healthy before orthognathic surgery; untreated disc displacement led to pain and 30% condylar resorption) and p99 (concomitant high condylectomy plus SSRO, or condylectomy as stage 1)
verified.explanation: Wolford treats the joints first or at the same operation. He reports that operating on jaws over untreated displaced discs led to worse pain and condylar resorption. The recalled answer follows Proffit's advice to defer TMJ surgery, which conflicts with this paper. Expect the exam key to follow Proffit.

stem: What is the appropriate retention protocol for a diastema that has been closed?
source_tag: proffit ch 19 (figure caption: fixed retainer of bonded 21.5-mil multistrand wire on the lingual of the central incisors; frenum surgery not performed)
proffit_chapter: Ch 19 Adult adjunctive treatment (special considerations in treatment for adults)

verified.answer: c. Fixed upper retainer (bonded, flexible)
verified.where: Melrose & Millett 1998, Type of retainer (p.511) and frenectomy paragraph (p.510); Zachrisson 1997 Prolonged Retention (PDF p.9, Joondeph & Riedel)
verified.explanation: Melrose says a closed median diastema needs a flexible fixed retainer, and that an abnormal frenum matters little for small diastemas (0.9–3.0 mm). Edwards' frenectomy, which also cuts transseptal fibres, reduces reopening, so option d is not baseless. Zachrisson lists marked adult median diastemas as an indication for permanent retention.

stem: The most compelling reason to start early headgear treatment is?
source_tag: 8, 4 Effectiveness of early orthopaedic treatment with headgear: a systematic review and meta-analysis, Spyridon N. Papageorgiou; 10, 3 Outcomes in a 2-phase randomized clinical trial of early Class II treatment, J. F. Camilla Tulloch

verified.answer: b. Reduce risk of trauma
verified.where: Table 5 p9; Discussion p10; Conclusions p10
verified.explanation: The skeletal gain shrinks long term. The PAR advantage disappears after phase 2 (MD −0.69, P=.53). Trauma during phase 2 fell (RR 0.34, NNT 9, moderate quality), which leaves trauma prevention as the lasting benefit. Tulloch 2004 (t09_3) supports the lack of lasting skeletal or occlusal benefit but does not report trauma.

stem: 15-year-old presented with lower crowding. What could be the factor?
source_tag: 5, 1 Changes in tooth size-arch length relationships from the deciduous to the permanent dentition: A longitudinal study, Samir E. Bishara

verified.answer: b. Decreased arch length
verified.where: Bishara 1999, 'Untreated Normals' (p.628); Little 1990 Abstract items 1–3 (p.235)
verified.explanation: This year Bishara's third-molar review carries the point: from 12 to 25 years the tooth size–arch length discrepancy grows (2.7 mm males, 3.5 mm females) because arch length falls steadily. The Bishara deciduous-to-permanent paper in the tag is not on this year's list. Little notes intercanine width also drops, but arch length is the factor named.

source_tag: 7, 2 Soft Tissue Changes Following the Extraction of Premolars in Nongrowing Patients With Bimaxillary Protrusion: A Systematic Review, Rosalia Leonardi

verified.where: Leonardi et al 2010 Abstract (p211) and Conclusions (p215); Table 4 (p214)
verified.explanation: Across the four included studies of nongrowing bimaxillary-protrusion patients, the lower lip retracted 2 to 4.5 mm after four-premolar extraction. The paper notes wide individual variation, especially for the lower lip.

stem: What is the relationship of periodontal health with a fixed retainer?
options: b. It will not affect periodontal health if the patient has good oral hygiene
source_tag: 19, 4 Orthodontic retention protocols: an evidence-based overview, Dalya Al-Moghrabi

verified.answer: a. Plaque and calculus (more plaque/calculus, rarely periodontal destruction)
verified.where: Al-Moghrabi et al 2021, 'What effect do fixed retainers have on periodontal health?' (p.774) and 'Are fixed retainers more likely to be associated with periodontal breakdown?' (p.775); Key points (p.770)
verified.explanation: Fixed retainers usually carry higher plaque and calculus, which seldom becomes periodontal breakdown. That is why they are reserved for patients with meticulous hygiene. Recession is a rare event (about 1%, with flexible spiral wire), not the usual relationship.

stem: One patient was given a lower fixed retainer and upper Hawley, while the other received upper and lower Essix. After 10 years, which of the following changes would be expected?
options: a. Occlusal outcome will be the same
recalled_answer: a. Occlusal outcome will be the same [underlined, with handwritten '?']
source_tag: 19, 4 Orthodontic retention protocols: an evidence-based overview, Dalya Al-Moghrabi

verified.answer: c. Alignment – better long-term lower incisor alignment expected with the fixed retainer (not stated in the paper for 10 years)
verified.where: Al-Moghrabi et al 2021, Key points (p.770); 'Are fixed or removable retention regimes more effective?' (p.774) and Table 4 (p.775); combination retainers (p.775)
verified.explanation: Fixed and vacuum-formed retainers perform alike short term (18 months), but fixed retainers held alignment better at 4 years, so differences appear over time. Equal occlusal contacts were shown only at short follow-up (1 year or less), and poor adherence (67% stopped by year 2) weakens removable regimens. No study reaches 10 years, so 'alignment' is the best inference, not a stated result.

stem: What is the best approach to prevent relapse of crowding of the lower incisors?
recalled_answer: b. IPR (circled); fiberotomies highlighted with note 'it's better in upper'

verified.where: Zachrisson 1997, 'Placing 2-2 Outside 3-3' (PDF p.3, Figs 5–6); IPR = Tuverson contact areas (PDF p.2–3, Fig 2); fiberotomy (PDF p.3)
verified.explanation: Zachrisson's measure written specifically for lower-incisor crowding relapse is to align the incisors as a block just outside the canine contacts. The 'better in upper' note on fiberotomy is correct. IPR is defensible but secondary: Zachrisson and Boese (in Melrose) use it alongside other measures, and an RCT in Al-Moghrabi found IPR similar to fixed retainers at 5 years. The item is therefore ambiguous; other years' recalls chose 'labial to canines'.

verified.explanation: Björk measured these two factors exactly this way (vertical condylar growth by the mandibular base-ramus angle, mandibular length from chin point to condylar head). Both are skeletal factors for lower third-molar impaction, and condylar growth direction ranks first.

verified.where: Kokich & Shapiro 1984 Case 4, p147-150 (scanned pages 9-10, 12); Case 2, p143-146, is similar
verified.explanation: Case 4 is a 25-year-old woman with sensitivity from root exposure (recession) on the upper centrals, and a Class II div 1 with maxillary protrusion. She was treated with upper first premolars plus the lower left central incisor, upper IPR, and high-pull headgear with a TPA. Case 3 (a 44-year-old Class II div 2 with periodontal disease) was the one that needed mandibular surgery, and it does not fit 'increased overjet'.

stem: (Early treatment of vertical skeletal dysplasia: the hyperdivergent phenotype) Patient with hyperdivergent pattern treated with lip bumper, bonded expander, lip seal and headgear; what is the treatment effect?
source_tag: last year article: Early treatment of vertical skeletal dysplasia: the hyperdivergent phenotype, pg 147 in summary file; note: bonded palatal expander functioned as a posterior bite-block, fixed throughout treatment

verified.answer: A net orthopedic improvement. True forward mandibular rotation was 2.7 times controls (1.6° vs 0.6°). Condylar growth increased (3.8 vs 2.6 mm) and was redirected anterosuperiorly. The gonial angle decreased (-1.1°), the chin moved forward about twice as much as in controls, and posterior facial height increased. Upper molars were relatively intruded by 1.0 mm and lower molar eruption was controlled. Overbite rose 1.3 mm (2.7 mm in the open-bite subgroup) and overjet fell. Expansion did not raise the mandibular plane angle.
verified.where: Abstract; Tables II-VI pp320-323; Discussion pp322-324; Conclusions pp324-325
verified.explanation: The stem says headgear, but the paper used a high-pull chincup (fitted in 30 of 38 patients, 79%), not headgear. The authors contrast their results with high-pull headgear, which lets the lower molars erupt. Patients started at 8.2 years and were treated for 1.3 years. Long-term stability was not tested.

stem: Father came to the clinic asking about the difference between 2 appliances (photos: bonded palatal expander with Crozat/lip bumper; molar force device with lip bumper supported anteriorly by a fabricated framework):
options: a. A gives more force than B
b. if B is positioned 2 mm it will give greater force
c. (other options not remembered in detail)

verified.answer: Neither recalled option is right. B (the shield lip bumper on Hodge's framework) gives more force than a wire bumper. Option b is false because force rises at 4 mm, not 2 mm, and the shield cannot sit at 2 mm.
verified.where: Hodge 1997 Fig 1B (p615), Methods (p614), Results (p615-616), Conclusions (p621); photo A is the Crozat/lip bumper with bonded palatal expander from t17_2 Fig 1
verified.explanation: Hodge's Fig 1B shows the shield bumper on the molar force device, and the shield beat the wire at every position tested. Hodge never tested a Crozat/BPE appliance, so the paper supports A > B only if A is read as a plain wire bumper, and then that option is false too. Moving the bumper forward (2 to 4 mm) or gingivally increases force, so option b is reversed.

stem: Patient 12 years old with Class II div 1, lisping and tongue thrust; what is your treatment option to improve the speech?

verified.explanation: If lisping and tongue thrust or malocclusion coexist before puberty, a speech clinician should start speech (articulation) therapy. Classic myofunctional therapy adds little and is contraindicated if the faucial isthmus is narrow. Orthodontics does not correct the speech.

stem: Patient has Class III with spacing and crossbite, with defects in the letters l, n, t, d and s; which malocclusion is related to the defect?

verified.where: Johnson & Sandy 1999, p307-308 Class III relationships (Laine: mesial mandibular dentition and medioalveolar consonants; 4.5x and 3.7x risk); p308 spacing and /l/, /n/, /d/; p308 Increased overbite (conflicting, Laine found no relationship)
verified.explanation: Mesial occlusion and mandibular overjet raised the risk of alveolar consonants being made too far forward, and Class III tongue posture impairs /s/. Together these cover l, n, t, d and s. Spacing explains only /l/, /n/, /d/, and increased overbite has no consistent link.

verified.where: Results p4–6; Table 3 p7; Table 5 p9; Discussion p10
verified.explanation: The review lists overjet among reported trauma risk factors, although the two included trials found no overjet–trauma link. Early headgear prevented about one injury for every nine children treated (moderate-quality evidence). Using the overall RR 0.68 also gives NNT 9 for an average patient and 6 for a high-risk one.

verified.where: AAO White Paper p23 'Treatment of pediatric OSA'; p26 Executive summary rec 4
verified.explanation: Enlarged tonsils and adenoids are the commonest pediatric OSA risk factor, and T&A is the usual first-line treatment. The paper says to use mandibular advancement only for a true retrognathic problem, and that it is not a substitute for removing the obstruction.

stem: Patient is a mouth breather with constricted maxilla; which treatment do you recommend?

verified.answer: a. Haas, 3 months retention (not stated in the paper as a recommendation). The 3-month retention is what Garib used, and Haas and Hyrax gave similar orthopedic and nasal-floor effects.
verified.where: t14_3 Abstract, Methods p549 (3-month retention), Tables 2-4 (NF changes), Discussion p556
verified.explanation: Garib found no orthopedic advantage for either appliance: nasal-floor width rose about one-third of the screw opening with both. So appliance type does not decide the question, and the retention period does. The papers in this topic support about 3 months (2-4 months in the review), not 6. The recalled answer (Hyrax, 6 months) is not backed by the topic's papers, so this question should be treated as uncertain.

stem: Patient with 21 mm distance from Xi to the 2nd molar; it is indicative of?

verified.explanation: Ricketts' cut-offs in Bishara make 20 mm or less inadequate and 30 mm or more sufficient. 21 mm is borderline, within the 2.8 mm standard error of the inadequate cut-off and far below the Saudi normal (29.04 mm) from the Habib article, which is not on this year's list. 'Impacted third molar' is the best-supported option, but the paper does not settle 21 mm exactly.

stem: Patient with Class II; two extraction patterns offered: all 4s, or upper 4s and lower 5s. What is true?

verified.explanation: Taking out lower first premolars retracted the lower incisors about 1.5-1.6 mm more than taking out lower second premolars, and this held after adjusting for starting incisor position. stem: Bisphosphonate:

verified.answer: Ricketts: predicted Xi point to distal of lower second molar along the occlusal plane (from head films at 8–9 y): ≥30 mm = enough space, ≤20 mm = inadequate (SE 2.8 mm, ~90% accuracy with Turley curves). Page 5 = the six consensus-conference points
verified.where: Bishara 1999, 'Prediction of Space Availability for Third Molar Eruption' (p.631 = PDF page 4); Consensus points 1–6 (p.632 = PDF page 5)
verified.explanation: The paper uses Xi point but never defines it; the 'centre of the ramus' definition comes from Ricketts. The six points: (1) lower crowding is multifactorial, so don't extract third molars only for it; (2) distalizing molars can impact third molars, so some may be removed before retraction; (3) third molars are not needed for basal bone growth; (4) removal is easier with roots about two-thirds formed; (5) no enucleation from 7–9-year predictions; (6) warn of risks (permanent >0.5%, transitory ≥5%).

stem: Articular disc: thick anterior and posterior borders act as wedges, giving the disc a self-seating capacity that prevents condyle displacement during translation
Closing (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid): the disc-condyle complex returns to its rest position moving upward and backward; the SLP contracts to stabilize the disc-condyle complex
The most frequent presenting symptom of TMD is pain (masticatory muscles, preauricular area and/or TMJ), aggravated by chewing
The masticatory system includes maxilla, mandible, the dentition with its supporting structures, and various muscles of the head and neck

Discal (collateral) ligaments: attach medial and lateral borders of the disc to the poles of the condyle; restrict the lower joint to hinge movement; can become inflamed and painful (vascularized and innervated)
Condyle and eminence: the condyle is convex anteroposteriorly; the eminence is convex in the sagittal plane
Superior lateral pterygoid (SLP): exerts a holding/bracing action on the condyle during power strokes (clenching, chewing hard objects) and holds the disc to the condyle
Posterior attachment: another name is retrodiscal tissue or bilaminar zone
source_tag: TMD course slide marked 'Q another name' (handwritten)

verified.answer: Unknown variable – no pretreatment factor predicts relapse
verified.where: Little 1990, Abstract item 5 (p.235); Results items 1–2 and 5 (p.236); Clinical Implications (p.239–240)
verified.explanation: In the University of Washington records, nothing predicted long-term relapse: not Angle class, retention length, age, sex, initial or final alignment, overbite, overjet, arch dimensions, cephalometric values, or combinations of these. stem: Patient came with chronic asthma. Patient's sister had orthodontic treatment and finished very quickly (OPG pre and post of sister with resorption of anterior teeth). What is the expected outcome?

verified.answer: Orthodontically induced root resorption
verified.where: Weltman 2010 p463 (genetic influences and asthma, refs 54 and 84, among patient risk factors); Burnheimer 2024 p1 (genetic SNPs and allergy)
verified.explanation: Two patient risk factors point to EARR: chronic asthma (listed by Weltman) and a sibling with RR, which suggests heritable susceptibility (Weltman's genetic factors; Burnheimer's ACTN3/TSC2 polymorphisms).

stem: Patient came with severe upper crowding and impacted right canine, extracted upper 4s, and finished treatment. What is the retention plan for this case?
proffit_chapter: Ch 18 Retention

verified.answer: Removable or fixed retainers
verified.where: Al-Moghrabi et al 2021, Key points and Abstract (p.770); 'For how long should retainers be worn?' (p.771); Conclusions (p.775–776)
verified.explanation: The review treats prolonged retention as routine, recommending either long-term fixed retention or long-term part-time removable wear. Fixed and removable retainers perform similarly in the short term and no single retainer is best. 'No retention' is not supported; fibrotomy is an adjunct for rotations, not a retention plan.

stem: Patient has decreased function of thyroid and takes thyroxine. What is the expected outcome?

verified.answer: Increased alveolar bone resorption/turnover (faster tooth movement), not increased root resorption
verified.where: Bartzela 2009, Thyroid hormones p22 and Discussion p24; Weltman 2010 p463 (hypothyroidism a risk factor) and ref 82 (thyroid administration to reduce RR)
verified.explanation: Bartzela says thyroxine raises bone turnover, can cause osteoporosis and speeds OTM. Weltman lists untreated hypothyroidism as an RR risk factor and cites thyroxine given to reduce RR. A treated hypothyroid patient therefore shows more bone resorption rather than more root resorption.

stem: Patient came with his mother and wanted to ask what's the difference between Hyrax+Facemask (RME+CFB) and Facemask expansion (CFB). Both expansion protocols retained 90% of the initial intermolar expansion 15 years after expansion. What is the most appropriate?

stem: Patient came with hyperdivergent mandible, sleep apnea, and adenoid obstruction. What's the appropriate treatment?

verified.where: AAO White Paper p23 (T&A first line); p26 Executive summary rec 4 (refer to ENT). Flores-Mir 2013 p274 and Table 1 (Zettergren-Wijk: near-normalisation 5 years after T/A)
verified.explanation: The white paper makes tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy the usual first-line treatment for pediatric OSA and tells orthodontists to refer adenotonsillar hypertrophy to ENT. The JADA review adds that clearing the obstruction can steer vertical growth back toward normal.

stem: 8-year-old patient that was treated with RPE. What's the expected treatment [outcome]?

stem: 8-year-old patient treated with Hyrax expansion and was instructed to activate twice daily. What's the expected adverse effect?
source_tag: numbered list 1–98, no header, article-based (p16–25); flagged *** in source

verified.answer: Nasal effects: the nasal-bone sutures open (internasal 0.6 mm, nasomaxillary 0.4 mm, frontonasal 0.2 mm). The paper calls this nasal widening; calling it 'nasal distortion' or an adverse effect is not stated in the paper.
verified.where: t14_1 Methods p512 (2 quarter turns twice daily, Hyrax, ages 8-15); Table I p518; Discussion p517
verified.explanation: Ghoneima's Hyrax protocol matches the stem: twice-daily activation in children aged 8-15. CT showed that the forces open the anterior and nasal sutures, while the zygomatic and pterygomaxillary sutures stay closed. The authors read the nasal changes as a wider nasal cavity rather than a harm. 'Nasal distortion' is the closest option, but the label comes from the exam (and possibly Proffit), not from this paper.

stem: 11-year-old patient came with bilateral crossbite. What's the ideal treatment?
proffit_chapter: Ch 13 Skeletal problems in preadolescent children (RPE)

verified.where: t14_3 Methods p549 (3-month retention, girls aged 11-14); Table 4 and Conclusions p556-557
verified.explanation: Garib treated girls aged 11-14 with bilateral or unilateral crossbite and kept the appliance for 3 months. Hyrax and Haas gave similar orthopedic results. Haas tipped the anchor first premolars more, and the Hyrax is easier to keep clean. Ghoneima and Marshall also use the Hyrax with about 3 months of retention. A quad-helix is mainly a dental expander.

stem: 10-year-old patient that was treated with early expansion. What is the expected outcome?

Long-term skull width, nasal, intermolar and orbital width

verified.explanation: A 10-year-old is before the peak. In the paper, the pre-peak RME group's only short-term advantage was nasal cavity width. In the long term they gained maxillary skeletal, maxillary intermolar, lateronasal and latero-orbital widths over controls. Lateronasal plus intermolar gains alone (options A/B) describe the late-treated group, so the highlighted short-term option does not match.

stem: Patient with subdivision class II left and was treated with headgear. What is the expected outcome?

verified.answer: Scissor bite on the right (Class I, no-stop side); crossbite tendency on the left (Class II, stop side)
verified.where: Results, inner-bow characteristic 4, p72; Discussion p74; Introduction p68
verified.explanation: With the inner bow lengthened on the left, up to about 30–40% of the extraoral force is lost to lateral forces and moments. The authors tie this to a scissor bite on the no-stop side and a crossbite on the stop side, so the right side goes toward scissor bite.

stem: Patient came and was treated with Kloehn headgear with upward angulation of the outerbow. What is the expected outcome?
recalled_answer: Backward and downward growth of the maxilla (highlighted); handwritten: Downward, Backward; 'Headgear for distalization'

verified.answer: Forward maxillary growth is held back (A point moves back, SNA falls) and the palatal plane rotates down and back (posteriorly); this rotation is largest with cervical (Kloehn) pull
verified.where: Papageorgiou Results p4, subgroup analysis p7, Discussion p9, Table 2 p5 (cervical trials with upward outer bows); Bilbo Introduction p2 (Melsen: cervical traction restricts and rotates the maxilla clockwise)
verified.explanation: Pooled trials show headgear moves A point back (SNA −1.63°/yr) and rotates the palatal plane posteriorly. Cervical headgear did this most (SMD 1.50 vs 0.11 for high-pull), but the rotation evidence is very low quality. The review could not test outer-bow inclination itself. The dental effect of an upward bow (distal root moment on the molar) is Proffit material.

The growth would be similar to untreated

stem: 24-year-old male patient with class II div 1 with severely retruded mandible, sleep apnea, and small upper and lower airway. He also snores at night and can't sleep well, and he is very enthusiastic about treatment. What is the best treatment?

verified.explanation: Surgery for an OSA patient with a sagittal skeletal discrepancy and an orthodontic indication points to MMA in the paper, and the small upper and lower airway also points to both jaws. Isolated mandibular advancement is not the paper's OSA operation. The paper still names CPAP as the gold standard, so CPAP is the answer if the item asks for first-line treatment.

stem: Patient came with class II div. 1 with lisping. The mother has it and stated the siblings also had speech therapy in the past. What could be the reason?

verified.answer: Genetics (not stated in the paper)
verified.where: Johnson & Sandy 1999, p306 (Harvold mechanism 2: genetic or metabolic CNS disorder); p307 (Blyth: Class II skeletal morphology little influence on lisping); p309 Conclusions
verified.explanation: When the mother and siblings share the speech problem, the paper's shared genetic/CNS mechanism explains both the lisp and the malocclusion better than the malocclusion causing the lisp. Class II/1 morphology had little effect on lisping, and the review finds no direct link between severity of malocclusion and misarticulation.

stem: Patient came with class III, reverse overjet, spacing, and problems with pronunciation of i, d, s, t. With family history of speech therapy. What could be the cause?

verified.explanation: Class III/mesial occlusion and spacing are each linked to alveolar consonant errors, but the family history of speech therapy is the deciding clue. It points to a shared genetic/CNS cause, Harvold's second mechanism. The paper offers this as a possible mechanism, not as a ruling on this case.

stem: Patient came with tongue thrust, malocclusion and speech difficulties. What is the most appropriate treatment?

verified.answer: Speech therapy by a speech clinician, started without waiting for orthodontics (myofunctional exercises only as an adjunct in pubertal patients)

verified.explanation: With tongue thrust, malocclusion and a speech problem together, the authors say a speech clinician should start articulation therapy and not delay it until orthodontics. Myofunctional therapy adds little before puberty and may help resting posture alongside ortho later.

stem: Patient came with crossbite and hyperdivergent mandible, and was treated with expander and Crozat lip bumper and chin-cup. What's the expected outcome?

stem: Patient with class II molar relationship, and can be treated with either extraction of upper and lower first premolars or upper first premolars and lower second premolars. What is the difference?

stem: Patient with class II. What's the difference between early and late treatment?

stem: Patient with periodontium problem treated with orthognathic surgery. Stabilizing archwire pre-surgical for 0.018 slot is:

stem: Case; patient came with severe lower incisor irregularity with normal molar relationships and lower midline shifted 4 mm to the left with Bolton lower anterior excess of 0.4 mm. What is the treatment?

stem: Patient with retruded maxilla and anterior crossbite. What is the best treatment?

stem: Case of class III patient with forward growth and counterclockwise mandibular rotation. What is the most appropriate cephalometric measurement to analyze the discrepancy for this case?

stem: Table of different values for Co-GD, Co-Goi, Co-Pg, and Ar-Goi-Me. What's the expected outcome?

stem: 22-year-old male patient came with class III and maxillary constriction, 2 mm crossbite on each side. What's the appropriate treatment?
